faqs.question: What is your learning journey?
faqs.answer: His journey started in 2022 with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. In 2023 he built his first real projects and learned Node.js and Express. In 2024 he adopted TypeScript and React and began studying cloud data engineering and Linux. Today he ships production-quality apps and is preparing for a career in cloud and full stack engineering.

faqs.question: What are you currently learning?
faqs.answer: Right now he's deepening his knowledge of Cloud Data Engineering — data pipelines, cloud platforms, MongoDB and Linux administration — while refining his TypeScript and full stack engineering skills.

faqs.question: What are your plans for the future?
faqs.answer: Next on his roadmap: mastering cloud data pipelines, deepening backend architecture skills, growing his open source presence and landing an impactful internship or role in cloud/full stack engineering.

faqs.question: How should I start learning web development?
faqs.answer: His advice: start with HTML and CSS, then JavaScript, then a backend like Node.js. Build small projects early — a personal page, a todo app, a weather app. Practice beats theory, and consistency beats intensity.

faqs.question: What resources do you recommend?
faqs.answer: He recommends freeCodeCamp for structured foundations, MDN for web documentation, official docs for frameworks, and building real projects. YouTube tutorials are great to start — but building is what makes you a developer.

faqs.question: What roadmap would you recommend?
faqs.answer:
A practical roadmap:

1. HTML & CSS — build static pages
2. JavaScript — the language of the web
3. Git & GitHub — version control
4. Node.js & Express — backend basics
5. A framework like React
6. Databases like MongoDB
7. Deployment & cloud basics

Then specialize: data engineering, devops or frontend architecture.

faqs.question: How long does it take to learn web development?
faqs.answer: It took him consistent daily practice — you can learn the basics in 3–6 months of focused effort, and become job-ready in 1–2 years with real projects. The key is consistency and building.

faqs.question: Self-taught or a degree?
faqs.answer: Both work! He does both: a Computer Science degree for fundamentals plus self-learning for practical skills. For most developers, your portfolio and projects matter more than where you studied.

faqs.question: What new technologies are you exploring?
faqs.answer: He's exploring cloud data pipelines, Linux administration, MongoDB, advanced TypeScript patterns, server-side rendering and AI-assisted development workflows with the OpenCode CLI.

faqs.question: How do you study every day?
faqs.answer: He keeps a daily habit of at least 30–60 minutes of focused learning — reading docs, watching a tutorial, solving a challenge or building a feature. Small daily progress compounds.

faqs.question: What was your hardest learning challenge?
faqs.answer: Understanding async JavaScript and backend architecture took him the longest — promises, callbacks, error handling and thinking server-side. He overcame it by building real APIs and debugging them relentlessly.

faqs.question: Do you solve coding challenges?
faqs.answer: Yes — he practices algorithms and data structures on platforms like freeCodeCamp, sharpening the problem-solving skills his CS degree emphasizes.

faqs.question: Do you learn in public?
faqs.answer: Yes — he shares his learning through his YouTube channel and open source work. Explaining what you learn is one of the fastest ways to truly learn it.

faqs.question: Do you have a mentor?
faqs.answer: His mentors are indirect: open source maintainers, tutorial creators and the developers he follows online. He also learns a lot by mentoring beginners — teaching sharpens his own skills.

faqs.question: How do you balance learning and building?
faqs.answer: The 70/30 rule: about 70% of his time goes to building real projects, and 30% to structured learning. You learn most by building — study just enough to unblock the next build.

faqs.question: Do you read tech books?
faqs.answer: Yes — he reads technical books and deep documentation for topics like JavaScript, TypeScript and cloud engineering, and follows docs as the source of truth for frameworks.

faqs.question: What skills do you want to learn next?
faqs.answer: His skill roadmap: advanced cloud architecture and data pipelines, infrastructure automation, deeper React and TypeScript patterns, and system design for scalable applications.

faqs.question: What failures taught you the most?
faqs.answer: His failed deployments and broken builds taught him the most — debugging production issues, writing tests, and reading error messages carefully. Every failure became a lesson in his toolkit.
